highlight.text: Six feet was not an unprecedented size for a painting; many other paintings were wider or taller. … However, paintings of this size were reserved for more 'important' subjects, such as historical, religious or mythological topics.

source.label: Museum record (Wikidata): oil paint on canvas

work.text: The painting marked a vital turning point in the artist's career. It was the first in a series of six so called 'six-footers', depicting scenes on the River Stour, which includes his celebrated work The Hay Wain.
There are generally in the life of an artist perhaps one, two or three pictures, on which hang more than usual interest – this is mine.

source.author: John Constable
source.title: Letter to John Fisher, 1826, quoted in “The White Horse (Constable)”

moment.text: He does not give a sentiment, a soul to the exterior of Nature, as Mr TURNER does; he does not at all exalt the spectator’s mind, which Mr TURNER eminently does, but he gives her outward look, her complexion and physical countenance, with more exactness.

moment.text: For the first time, an artist was using extra-ordinary proportions for the most ordinary of English scenes

source.author: Nicola Moorby
source.title: Turner and Constable: Art, Life, and Landscape (2025), quoted in “The White Horse (Constable)”

matters.text: Constable was voted an Associate of the Royal Academy on the strength of it. The painting was purchased for 100 guineas by Constable's friend John Fisher
This purchase finally provided Constable with financial security and it’s arguable that without it, he may have given up painting altogether.
